results.title: Nscale Posts $1.02B Net Loss in H1, Nebius GPU Rental Rates Rise Up to 21% | BroadChain.info
highlights:
AI cloud service provider Nebius announced that starting October 1, it will raise on-demand rental prices for some Nvidia GPUs, the second price increase within three months. The price per GPU hour for H100 rose from $3.85 to $4.50, an increase of about 17%; H200 rose from $4.50 to $5.40, an increase of 20%; B200 and B300 rose to $8.50 and $9.50 respectively. This price adjustment also involves some CPU and memory resources. Nebius recently signed four customer contracts averaging more than $1 billion each, and competitor CoreWeave also said prices for newly signed computing power contracts have increased. However, this adjustment targets on-demand quotes for designated regions and models, and long-term reservation customers can still obtain discounts.

 Today's main thread: GPU rental prices are still rising, but the funds needed for computing power expansion are also becoming increasingly massive. Nebius once again raised on-demand quotes, OpenAI expects free cash flow outflow of $278 billion over the next five years, and Oracle-related data center loans are seeing discounts and distribution difficulties. There are still pricing signals on the demand side, but whether projects can obtain funding, be delivered on schedule, and generate revenue will affect subsequent expansion.

James Okafor September 19, 2026

Cloud provider Nebius will raise pay-as-you-go prices for leasing selected Nvidia chips starting October 1, the company said on Thursday, September 17, in comments reported by Reuters and carried by Economic Times Tech. It is the company's second price increase in three months. [1]

Rates for selected Nvidia graphics processing units will rise between 17% and 21%, according to the report. On-demand rates for some central processing units made by AMD and Intel, along with memory offerings, are also going up: the company said prices of some CPU-only instances will rise by 25% and memory offerings by about 41%. Customers reserving large-scale clusters for multiple months can receive commitment discounts. [1]

Neocloud companies such as Nebius rent out the high-powered chips and data centre infrastructure used to train and run AI models. Demand for that capacity is surging, per the report, and rival CoreWeave said earlier the same day that it is signing contracts at higher prices. [1]

results.title: Nebius augmente de 21 % les prix de location des GPU face à l’envolée de la demande en infrastructures d’IA | Gate News
highlights:
- Nebius a annoncé une hausse de 21 % des prix de location des GPU à partir du 1er octobre 2024, après la hausse de 30 % de juin.
- Le prix de location à la demande du B300 de Nebius a augmenté de 56 % au total sur cinq mois.
- Oracle a renouvelé tous les contrats de GPU arrivés à expiration à des tarifs supérieurs de 20 % au cours de son trimestre précédent.

Le fournisseur de location de GPU Nebius a annoncé qu’il augmenterait jusqu’à 21 % les prix de location de GPU à la demande à partir du 1er octobre, selon un rapport publié le 22 septembre par Park Jae-hwan, analyste chez Eugene Investment & Securities. Cette hausse fait suite à une augmentation de 30 % des prix de l’ensemble des gammes de GPU le 1er juin, portant ainsi à environ 56 % en près de cinq mois la hausse du prix de location à la demande du B300 de Nebius. Eugene Investment attribue cette escalade continue des prix à la forte demande en infrastructures d’IA, dans un contexte d’intensification de la concurrence entre les développeurs de modèles d’IA. Oracle a également renouvelé au trimestre précédent tous ses contrats de GPU arrivés à expiration à des tarifs supérieurs de 20 %.

## Nebius met en œuvre une deuxième hausse des prix des GPU en cinq mois

Nebius a décidé d’augmenter jusqu’à 21 % les prix de location de GPU à la demande à compter du 1er octobre, marquant la deuxième hausse depuis le 1er juin, date à laquelle l’entreprise avait augmenté de 30 % les prix de l’ensemble de sa gamme de GPU. Park Jae-hwan a indiqué que le prix de location à la demande du B300 de Nebius avait augmenté d’environ 56 % en près de cinq mois à la suite de ces ajustements successifs.

## Oracle renouvelle ses contrats de GPU avec une prime de 20 %

La tendance à la hausse des prix de location dépasse le cadre de Nebius. Oracle a révélé, lors de l’annonce de ses résultats du trimestre précédent, avoir renouvelé tous les contrats de GPU arrivés à expiration à des prix supérieurs de 20 % aux tarifs précédents. Park a déclaré que la prise en compte simultanée des hausses des prix de location sur les marchés spot et contractuels indiquait une accélération de la croissance des revenus des entreprises de néo-cloud et confirmait une nouvelle fois la vigueur de la demande en infrastructures d’IA.

results.title: GPU price index 2026: cloud rental surge versus retail volatility | SpecForge
highlights:
1. Cloud GPU rental prices for the newest cohort rose from $2.12/hr in October 2024 to $4.72/hr by September 2026, while Legacy silicon fell from $1.77 to $0.95 over the same window, per the AIMultiple index covering 17 models across 75 providers [S4].
2. Retail-side GPU tracking is dominated by Tom's Hardware's daily price index and Semianalysis's cloud-rental composite [S1][S2].

...

The newest-generation cloud GPU cohort (B200, B300, MI300X, RTX 5090) saw on-demand median hourly rental rise from $2.12 in October 2024 to $4.72 in September 2026, while the Modern cohort (H100, H200, A100, L40S, RTX 4090, A10G, T4, L4) moved from $1.35 to $1.45 over the same period [S4].

The Legacy silicon cohort (V100, P100, K80, M60, P40) saw its on-demand median hourly rental fall from $1.77 in October 2024 to $0.95 in September 2026 [S4]. The divergence is the dominant signal in the 2026 GPU pricing landscape.

...

The AIMultiple index groups 17 tracked SKUs into three fixed cohorts to keep the time series comparable even as individual listings churn [S4]. Each GPU contributes equally to its group median, so a single provider's price cut does not skew the cohort. The Last released cohort (2024 and later) has the steepest curve: B200 and B300 medians now sit at $6.52 and $7.87 per GPU-hour on-demand, while MI300X runs at $2.91, undercutting H100 at $3.25 [S4]. RTX 5090 at $0.63 and RTX 4090 at $0.44 reflect consumer-card economics entering the rental pool, with the 4090 still widely available at 68% of tracked listings and the 5090 at 79% [S4].

MI ... 00X reserved pricing reverses the usual ... : its reserved ... of $3.39 sits above the $2.9 ... on-demand median, a signal that long-term MI300X ... scarce enough ... premium ... B300 ... s reserved median of $ ... . ... 1 against its ... 7.87 on ... demand still delivers ... 27 ... discount ... terms [ ... 4].

...

## Provider-level dispersion: H200 ranges from $2.09 to $13.78

GPU price history and index - Provider-level dispersion: H200 ranges from $2.09 to $13.78

Provider choice adds a second axis of price variation. September 2026 H200 on-demand listings span $2.09 per GPU-hour at Beam to $13.78 at Microsoft Azure, a 6.6x spread that reflects differences in instance configuration, stock state, and data-residency tier rather than raw hardware markup [S4]. IONOS prices H100 and H200 as flat $3,990 monthly dedicated servers with EU data residency, a billing model that hides the hourly rate but is competitive against the $3.25 to $4.40 hourly H100/H200 medians for buyers needing residency guarantees [S4].

Cloud GPU pricing has bifurcated between hyperscalers (Azure, AWS, GCP) anchoring the high end with full-managed services and neoclouds (Beam, RunPod, Vast, Lambda) anchoring the low end with bare-metal or spot capacity. The price gap is widest on H200, narrowest on commodity cards like T4 and L4 where multiple providers converge near cost-of-power-plus-amortization [S4].

...

Hourly rental rate alone does not measure workload cost. The 2026 GPU index recommends pairing the rental table with a multi-GPU benchmark covering H100, H200, B200, and MI300X to compute time-to-completion on representative training and inference workloads [S4]. A 1.8x faster GPU at 1.5x the hourly rate is cheaper per job, a calculation that flipped H200's value proposition in 2025 once NVLink and FP8 throughput differences were measured on production transformer training rather than peak FLOPS [S4].

...

The AIMultiple index computes each median from listings present in the given month, so provider and SKU turnover can shift the median even without an underlying rate change [S4]. Physical variants sold under the same model name (A100 40GB versus 80GB, H100 PCIe versus SXM versus NVL) are combined unless the source explicitly separates them by memory or interconnect [S4]. Semianalysis applies a composition-jump-resistant weighted mean specifically to suppress this kind of turnover noise, at the cost of a less transparent per-GPU median [S2].

...

For a hyperscale or neocloud capacity buyer, the dominant 2026 signal is the 122% rise in newest-cohort on-demand pricing against flat Modern pricing, which means the cost of stepping up to B200/B300 has roughly doubled since late 2024 while the cost of staying on H100/A100 has not [S4]. The H200 6.6x provider spread ($2.09 to $13.78) is the next-most-actionable number, because a workload that runs acceptably on H200 can be cost-cut by 5-6x simply by changing provider, with residency and managed-service features as the trade-off [S4].

results.title: Cloud GPU Price Index: weekly median listed on-demand price of one NVIDIA H100 GPU-hour
highlights: Canonical source: https://gpueconomy.com/price-index, recomputed hourly. This record is a dated snapshot (version 2026-09-19, data updated 2026-09-19T09:26:26.511913+00:00) so that a cited number keeps existing exactly as it was cited. Please cite GPU Economy and link the page. The index is the weekly median publicly listed on-demand price of one NVIDIA H100 SXM GPU-hour across the cloud GPU providers tracked by GPU Economy, in US dollars per GPU per hour, with a chain-linked base-100 companion series that moves only when a provider changes a listed price. Two files, two panels, never merged: price-index.csv is GPU Economy's own series, read hourly from each provider's price page from the week of 2026-09-07 (2 weeks in this version); price-index-history.csv is a second-hand series reconstructed from the public skypilot-org/skypilot-catalog (Apache 2.0) for the weeks before that (88 weeks, at most 7 providers). price-index.json carries the current week's constituents with the source URL behind every quote. Method: median, not mean, over one quote per provider and region (a provider that lists several regions enters once per region, and weighting_check in the JSON recomputes each week as a median of per-provider medians); on-demand rates only, spot and reserved excluded; node-priced offers divided by GPU count; USD-listed quotes only; marketplace floors excluded; a week is published only when at least 8 providers contributed. Full method: https://gpueconomy.com/methodology. Field definitions are in the README included with the files.

results.title: Best Cloud GPU for AI: Price Comparison (2026)
highlights:
The best cloud GPU for AI work is decided by one number before anything else: what an hour of compute costs. The same NVIDIA H100 rents for under two dollars an hour on a marketplace and about eleven dollars an hour on a hyperscaler. Same chip. Same 80 GB of memory. A gap of five times or more, and it’s got nothing to do with performance. It’s about where you rent it.

...

Strip away the marketing and there are really only three pricing models in this market, plus three kinds of seller.

On-demand is the default: a published hourly rate, yours until you stop it. Spot, also called preemptible, rents spare capacity at 50 to 80 percent off, but the provider can reclaim it with little warning. It suits checkpointed training, and it’s fatal for anything that can’t be interrupted. If you’re hunting for the best cloud GPU for AI on a tight budget, spot is usually where the search ends; most practitioners who rent H100 capacity by the hour learned that first. Reserved pricing trades a commitment of one month to three years for roughly 30 to 60 percent off.

Sellers fall into three camps. Hyperscalers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) sell GPUs inside giant cloud ecosystems: expensive per hour, but with compliance certifications, private networking, and tooling enterprises already run on. Neoclouds (Lambda, CoreWeave, RunPod, Nebius, Crusoe) are GPU-first companies built around AI workloads, typically 40 to 60 percent cheaper than hyperscalers on identical NVIDIA hardware. Marketplaces (Vast.ai and similar) let independent hosts list spare GPUs: the cheapest option by far, with variable reliability and no meaningful support.

Prices are quoted per GPU-hour and move constantly. Recent snapshots put the volume-weighted H100 average in the mid-three-dollars range; the cheapest advertised on-demand rates sit near $1.79 while hyperscaler listings reach roughly $11. That’s the pricing landscape every best cloud GPU for AI buyer is navigating. Treat every figure below as a recent snapshot, and check live cloud GPU pricing before a long run.

## Best cloud GPU for AI: the 8 providers, compared

All prices below are on-demand per-GPU-hour from recently published best cloud GPU for AI comparisons. Marketplace figures are ranges because hosts set their own prices. The H200 column matters more than it used to: NVIDIA’s 141 GB card is now the default recommendation for memory-bound inference.

| Provider | Type | H100 80GB ($/hr) | H200 141GB ($/hr) | A100 80GB ($/hr) | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lambda Labs | Neocloud | $3.29-$3.99 | — | $1.99-$2.79 | Straightforward ML-ready rentals |
| RunPod | Neocloud | $2.89-$2.99 | ~$4.59 | $1.00-$1.49 | Iterative experiments |
| Vast.ai | Marketplace | ~$1.40-$2.10 | — | from ~$0.53 | Cheapest possible prototyping |
| CoreWeave | Neocloud | $6.16 | ~$6.30 | ~$2.70 | Enterprise-scale training |
| Nebius | Neocloud | ~$3.85 | ~$4.50 | — | European data residency |
| Crusoe Cloud | Neocloud | ~$3.90 | — | — | Clean-energy procurement |
| AWS | Hyperscaler | ~$6.88 | ~$7.91 | ~$3.43 | Teams already on AWS |
| Google Cloud | Hyperscaler | ~$11.00 | ~$10.60 | — | GCP-native teams |

One more thing the table hides: the minimum purchase unit. CoreWeave’s $6.16 headline rate is node-locked to 8-GPU minimums, which is $49.24 an hour for the node, with no self-serve single-GPU option. Nebius at $3.85 and Lambda at $3.99 both allow single-GPU provisioning. If your job needs two GPUs, the effective per-GPU cost on CoreWeave’s on-demand tier jumps past $24. The headline rate is not the price. The minimum unit is part of the price. Any best cloud GPU for AI shortlist that ignores the minimum unit is comparing fiction.

...

Google Cloud’s list prices reach roughly $11 an hour on-demand for top H100 instances, though committed-use discounts cut that sharply. Same logic as AWS: the premium buys the ecosystem, including TPU workloads for GCP-native teams, not faster NVIDIA silicon. One caution: verify the rate on the provider’s own pricing page before budgeting. Stale launch-era figures still circulate, and the gap between an old number and today’s rate can double the apparent cost difference.

...

### How much does it cost to rent an H100 per hour?

Recent snapshots show on-demand H100 rates from about $1.79 an hour at the cheapest specialists to roughly $11 at hyperscalers, averaging in the mid-three-dollars range. To rent H100 capacity on a neocloud, expect roughly $2.89 to $3.99; RunPod, Lambda, and Nebius all sit in that band, and those are the bands that matter in any best cloud GPU for AI price comparison. Spot and marketplace rates go lower. Prices move, so check live rates before a long run.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Dataset
highlights: A free, openly licensed (CC BY 4.0) dataset of posted cloud GPU rental prices across the whole market: GPU marketplaces, specialized GPU clouds, serverless platforms and hyperscale clouds. It contains a normalized snapshot of every current posted offer (provider, GPU model, VRAM, offer type, region, per-GPU-hour price, minimum GPU count, availability) and a daily price series with each day's lowest, average and highest posted price per provider and GPU. Every price is a rate a provider publishes. None is a transaction. This version (2026-10-04) holds the snapshot of 2026-10-04 06:50 UTC and the daily series from 2026-08-05 to 2026-10-04. It is the first version to carry corrections: three labelling errors found on 2026-10-03 (a preemptible rate recorded as on-demand at one provider, a PCIe card recorded under the SXM name at two) are listed in corrections.json, the daily series is published both corrected (gpu-prices-daily) and exactly as recorded (gpu-prices-daily-as-recorded), and no assumed price is filled in. Earlier versions hold days back to 2026-07-31 and predate these corrections. It also archives FastGPU's comment to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission on the Request for Comment on the Listing of Compute Derivatives Contracts (RIN 3038-AF77, 91 FR 54259), together with the script, inputs and output that reproduce every figure in that comment (cftc-rin-3038-AF77-replication.zip). Published and maintained by FastGPU, a live GPU price comparison service. Official dataset page and column documentation: https://fastgpu.co/dataset. Method: https://fastgpu.co/methodology.
